issues.legal_issue: Omitting or relinquishing one of several distinct causes of action does not bar a later claim based on that distinct cause under the rule against splitting claims.
material_facts: The landlord initially sought eviction on three distinct grounds, then withdrew the personal-need and repair grounds before the tenant had been served or participated.
The landlord later sought to restore the personal-need ground in the same proceedings after withdrawing the ground based on her husband's need to leave government accommodation.
The tenant objected that restoring the personal-need ground was barred by the rule against splitting claims.
issues.conclusion: The later amendment was not barred because the personal-need ground was a distinct cause of action from the other grounds.
issues.legal_principle: Order II Rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies when a plaintiff omits or relinquishes part of a claim arising from the same cause of action; it does not prevent a later suit or claim based on a separate and distinct cause of action. The Court applied the principles in Mohammad Khalil Khan v. Mahbub Ali Khan, including that the causes of action are distinct where the claims rest on different facts or evidence.

predicates.eviction_proceeding: A landlord pursued a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.distinct_causes_of_action: The landlord's eviction grounds rested on separate and distinct causes of action.
predicates.cause_relinquished_before_opponent_parti: The landlord relinquished the cause later claimed before the tenant had participated in the proceeding.

issues.definition: When an eviction claim rests on distinct causes of action and one is relinquished before the tenant participates, a later claim based on that distinct cause is not barred.

issues.legal_issue: Constructive res judicata does not bar a later claim when the relinquishment of the earlier ground was not followed by a final adjudication between the parties.
material_facts: The landlord relinquished the relevant eviction ground before the tenant had participated in the proceeding.
No adjudication between the landlord and tenant had occurred when that ground was relinquished.
The landlord later sought to reintroduce the ground by amendment in the same proceedings.
issues.conclusion: Constructive res judicata did not bar the amendment because there had been no adjudication between the parties when the ground was relinquished.
issues.legal_principle: An essential condition for res judicata is a final adjudication between the parties after a hearing. Because the tenant was not yet involved and the matter had not been adjudicated when the ground was relinquished, the doctrine did not apply.

predicates.eviction_proceeding: A landlord pursued a proceeding seeking eviction of a tenant.
predicates.no_final_adjudication_between_parties: The parties had not received a final adjudication on the relinquished ground.

issues.definition: In an eviction proceeding, a later claim is not barred by constructive res judicata when the relinquished ground was never finally adjudicated between the parties.

issues.legal_issue: A special summary procedure for eviction on a landlord's bona fide personal-need grounds is not unconstitutional discrimination or an excessive delegation of power when the classification is reasonably connected to its purpose and safeguards remain available to the tenant.
material_facts: The tenant challenged the special eviction procedure as discriminatory because it differed from the procedure available for other eviction grounds.
The special procedure applied to eviction claims based on a landlord's bona fide personal need and was intended to provide quicker relief in such cases.
A tenant could obtain leave to defend by disclosing facts that would defeat the landlord's claim.
The procedure allowed revision by the High Court and review by the Controller in the circumstances specified by the statute.
issues.conclusion: The special procedure was constitutionally valid: it did not violate Article 14 or involve excessive delegation of power.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits hostile discrimination, not reasonable classification; a classification is permissible when it rests on an intelligible distinction with a rational connection to the legislative objective. The Court applied the presumption of constitutionality and the requirement that a challenger plead and prove the necessary facts. It relied on Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri v. Union of India, State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar, Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S.R. Tendolkar, Mahant Moti Das v. S.P. Sahi, and A.C. Aggarwal v. Mst. Ram Kali. It considered the procedure under Section 25B for claims under Section 14A and clause (e) of the proviso to Section 14(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, and referred to Bega Begum v. Abdul Ahmed Khan concerning the meaningful application of bona fide personal-need grounds.

predicates.procedure_limited_to_personal_need_cases: The special procedure applied to eviction cases based on the landlord's bona fide personal need rather than all eviction grounds.

issues.definition: A special procedure limited to personal-need eviction cases is constitutionally valid when its classification serves prompt relief and tenants retain a fact-based opportunity to defend and access to review.
